subsection: 2. The second Sinn Féin, the 1918 election and the War of Independence, 1917–1921

notes.b: The second Sinn Féin grew out of the 1916 Rising and the collapse of the older nationalist politics. A few pieces of background explain why Irish opinion moved so fast after 1916.
points: The Rising began on Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, and its leaders were executed in May 1916. The executions turned opinion towards the rebels, who had been widely unpopular until then.

The British called the Rising the 'Sinn Féin rebellion', and survivors and the public took up the name, so 'Sinn Féin' became a label for the Rising and everyone who supported it, even though the party had played little part.

Before 1916 the Irish Parliamentary Party (IPP), led by John Redmond, dominated nationalist politics and sought Home Rule (self-government within the United Kingdom) by constitutional means. It lost ground after 1916 because the rebels seemed to have achieved more than years of parliamentary work.

The Irish Volunteers (founded 1913) and the secret Irish Republican Brotherhood (IRB) were the physical-force organisations behind the Rising, and the Volunteers later became the IRA. This is why the IRA later drew on the same men.

Britain governed Ireland from Dublin Castle through the Lord Lieutenant (the Viceroy, the crown's representative), the Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC, an armed police force) and the Dublin Metropolitan Police (DMP). This is why attacks on the police and the Castle were attacks on British rule itself.
World War I ended with the Armistice on 11 November 1918. Britain's desperate need for soldiers in the last year of the war is what caused the conscription crisis of 1918.
notes.tip: For a Higher essay on self-government 1912-1921, place the second Sinn Féin and the IRA campaign as the third route, after Home Rule and the 1916 Rising.

notes.h: Key concepts: republic, sovereignty, abstention and the IRB/IRA
notes.b: Four ideas run through this period, and examiners expect you to use them precisely. Each one is a demand Sinn Féin made or a method it used.
points: A republic is a state with no monarch as head of state. Sinn Féin demanded one from 1917 and the Dáil declared one in 1919.

Sovereignty is supreme authority over a state's own affairs, with no other power able to override it. The Dáil claimed sovereignty over Ireland in the Declaration of Independence, which is why it set up its own government and courts.
Abstention means refusing to attend. Sinn Féin MPs refused to take their seats at Westminster, the British parliament, and sat in their own assembly, the Dáil, instead.

The IRB (Irish Republican Brotherhood) was a secret society. The IRA (Irish Republican Army) was the Volunteers' fighting force, owing allegiance to the Dáil, so it claimed to be the army of an elected government.
notes.tip: Define these terms as they are used in 1917-1921: a republic means no monarch, and abstention means sitting in the Dáil, not Westminster.

notes.h: The original Sinn Féin and the 1917 by-elections
notes.b: Sinn Féin was a small party before 1916. In 1917 a run of by-elections (elections held to fill a single vacant seat) showed that separatists, who wanted a complete break with Britain, could beat the IPP.
points: Arthur Griffith founded the first Sinn Féin in 1905. It stood for economic self-reliance, abstention from Westminster and a dual monarchy of Britain and Ireland on the Austro-Hungarian model, which is very different from the republic the party wanted by 1917.

Count Plunkett, father of the executed Joseph Plunkett, won the North Roscommon by-election in February 1917 as an independent separatist and then abstained from Westminster. His win showed that the rebels' cause had public support.
Joseph McGuinness, a prisoner in Lewes, won South Longford in May 1917 by 37 votes, helped by the slogan 'Put him in to get him out'. This showed that a prisoner could be a successful candidate.
De Valera won East Clare in July 1917 by a large majority, and W.T. Cosgrave won Kilkenny City in August 1917, so the successes were repeated in different parts of the country.
Together the four results showed that separatists could win seats from the IPP and that voters would back men who were in jail or had fought in 1916.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Griffith's first Sinn Féin of 1905, with its dual monarchy, with the second Sinn Féin of 1917, which wanted a republic under de Valera.

notes.h: Ashe's funeral, the October 1917 Ard Fheis and the growth of Sinn Féin
notes.b: A martyr and a new constitution turned a set of election victories into a movement. The Ard Fheis (the party's annual conference) of October 1917 gave it a leader and a united aim.
points: Thomas Ashe, one of the 1916 leaders, died on 25 September 1917 after being forcibly fed during a hunger strike in Mountjoy prison. His funeral drew huge crowds and became a rallying point for the movement.
Michael Collins spoke at the graveside, which marked his rise among the republicans.

At the Sinn Féin Ard Fheis of 25-26 October 1917 de Valera was elected president, with Griffith standing aside. De Valera also became president of the Volunteers that month, so political and military leadership was joined in one man.

The new constitution was a compromise: the aim was an independent Irish republic, and once that was achieved the people could choose their own form of government. This allowed republicans and Griffith's followers, who wanted a monarchy, to stay in one party.

Sinn Féin now drew in ex-Volunteers, the IRB, Gaelic Leaguers (supporters of the Irish-language revival) and many younger priests, and its clubs spread through the country. The IPP, by contrast, seemed discredited.
notes.tip: Do not mix up de Valera's two titles: president of Sinn Féin from October 1917, and later Príomh Aire (head of the Dáil ministry) from April 1919.

notes.h: The conscription crisis and the German Plot, 1918
notes.b: Conscription (compulsory military service) united nearly all Irish nationalist opinion against the government and gave Sinn Féin credit for leading the resistance.
points: The German spring offensive began in March 1918 and Britain was desperately short of men, so the Military Service Act of 18 April 1918 allowed conscription in Ireland.

An all-party anti-conscription conference met at the Mansion House in Dublin on 18 April, with Dillon, de Valera, Griffith, William O'Brien, Tim Healy and Labour representatives. The Catholic bishops, meeting at Maynooth, backed resistance, which gave it moral weight.
A national pledge to resist conscription was signed at church doors on 21 April, and on 23 April a one-day general strike closed most of the country outside Belfast.

The government never applied conscription, but it replaced the Viceroy with Lord French in May 1918. It also arrested about 70 Sinn Féin leaders on the claim of a 'German Plot' (a supposed plot with Germany), citing the landing of Joseph Dowling from a German submarine as its pretext.
De Valera, Griffith, Count Plunkett and Markievicz were among those held in Britain, while Collins and Harry Boland avoided arrest.
The arrests removed the older leaders and strengthened the radicals. Sinn Féin won by-elections in the summer, and Redmond's party, weakened by Redmond's death on 6 March 1918, lost ground.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on this crisis, say what the Act was, who resisted, what happened in May 1918 and why Sinn Féin gained, with a date for each statement. Do not confuse the 1918 German Plot, a British claim, with Casement's real mission to Germany in 1916.

notes.b: The first election after the end of the war was fought on a franchise (the right to vote) that roughly tripled the electorate, and it transformed the Irish party system.
points: The Representation of the People Act 1918 gave the vote to all men over 21 and women over 30, and the Irish electorate rose from about 700,000 to about 1.9 million.
The election was held on 14 December 1918 and counted on 28 December. Sinn Féin won 73 of Ireland's 105 seats, the Unionists won 26 and the Irish Parliamentary Party won only six.
Sinn Féin took about 47 per cent of the votes, and 25 of its seats were won without a contest (uncontested, because no rival stood).
The IPP was almost wiped out, but Joe Devlin held a Belfast seat.
Unionists won most of the seats in the north-east, so Belfast and Ulster supplied the evidence for partition.
Constance Markievicz won St Patrick's, Dublin, while in Holloway prison, and became the first woman elected to the House of Commons. She did not take her seat, in line with the policy of abstention.

De Valera was elected for East Clare and East Mayo, and many successful Sinn Féin candidates were in prison. This meant the Sinn Féin benches in the Dáil would be thin, so few could attend its first meeting.

Sinn Féin had promised to abstain and set up an Irish assembly, so the result gave it a mandate for that. It showed a vote for a republic and against the IPP, but with only about 47 per cent of votes, not every voter backed Sinn Féin.
notes.tip: Examiners reward the franchise change, the date, and the seat numbers for Sinn Féin, the Unionists and the IPP. The first woman elected to the Commons is Markievicz.

notes.b: Sinn Féin kept its election promise to set up its own parliament instead of going to Westminster. The Dáil (the Irish assembly) then began to behave like a government.
points: The First Dáil met at the Mansion House, Dublin, on 21 January 1919, but only 27 of the elected deputies attended because many were in jail.

It adopted three documents: a Declaration of Independence, a Message to the Free Nations of the World and the Democratic Programme. The Programme put the nation's claim to its resources and the right of every citizen to a living above private property.
De Valera escaped from Lincoln Gaol on 3 February 1919 with help from Collins and Boland, and was elected Príomh Aire (head of the Dáil ministry) on 1 April 1919.
The ministry included Griffith (Home Affairs), Collins (Finance), Cathal Brugha (Defence), Count Plunkett (Foreign Affairs) and Markievicz (Labour).
Remember that the First Dáil and the shooting at Soloheadbeg both took place on 21 January 1919, but they were separate events.
notes.tip: Short answers ask where the First Dáil met (the Mansion House) and what was set up in January 1919 (the Dáil, with its Declaration of Independence).

notes.b: A counter-state is a rival government that takes over the work of the official one. Between 1919 and 1921 the Dáil built one alongside Dublin Castle, which is what made its claim to sovereignty real.
points: The Dáil Loan (the National Loan), organised by Collins from 1919, raised over £350,000 in Ireland and more than 5 million dollars in the United States. These are two distinct sums, so do not add them up or confuse them.

Sinn Féin won most of the councils in the 1920 local elections, and local authorities then pledged loyalty to the Dáil, which cut Dublin Castle off from local government. This gave it local power, so the Dáil's authority reached into every county where it held the council.

The Dáil set up arbitration courts in 1919, which developed into Dáil courts from mid-1920, and republican police replaced the RIC in many areas. People used them because they were quick and had the backing of the community.
The British banned the Dáil in September 1919, and in 1920 many of the republican ministers worked in hiding.
From August 1920 the Volunteers swore an oath of allegiance to the Dáil, which tied the army to the elected government. The name IRA was in general use during the war.
notes.tip: The Dáil Loan raised money in Ireland and a separate sum in the United States, so give both figures and name Collins as the organiser.

notes.h: The IRA campaign begins: Soloheadbeg, barracks and flying columns
notes.b: The IRA waged a guerrilla war (small-scale surprise attacks rather than open battles) on the RIC and the army. A few thousand active men tied down many times their number.
points: The first shots came at Soloheadbeg, Co. Tipperary, on 21 January 1919, when Seán Treacy, Dan Breen and others killed two RIC constables guarding gelignite (an explosive). The Dáil had not ordered the attack. It is often seen as the start of the war.

The RIC withdrew from many isolated barracks in 1919-20, because they were hard to defend, and the IRA burned the empty buildings and attacked others. So the IRA could attack, for example, the barracks that remained.

Active service units, known as flying columns, ambushed patrols and barracks and then dispersed into the countryside. Tom Barry's West Cork column was the best known. This worked, for example, because a small column could vanish among local supporters.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on the war, start with Soloheadbeg on 21 January 1919 and state that the Dáil had not ordered it.

notes.h: Collins's intelligence war and the deaths of 1920
notes.b: Collins understood that in a war against a much larger force, information mattered more than numbers. Three deaths in 1920 also moved opinion against the British.
points: Collins was Director of Intelligence and used moles (informers inside the enemy's own offices) in Dublin Castle and the police, such as Ned Broy, a Dublin Castle clerk, to get information.
His Squad, formed in 1919, killed detectives of the DMP's G Division, the political branch of the Dublin police, and other agents. This blinded the British intelligence service in Dublin.
Tomás Mac Curtain, Lord Mayor of Cork, was murdered by police in March 1920, and Terence MacSwiney, his successor, died on hunger strike in Brixton prison on 25 October 1920.
Kevin Barry, an 18-year-old medical student, was hanged on 1 November 1920 for his part in an ambush that killed three soldiers. Because of his age, his death turned many people against the British.
notes.tip: Examiners expect Collins's roles to be named: Director of Intelligence, the Squad, and Ned Broy's information from Dublin Castle.

notes.h: Bloody Sunday, Kilmichael and the Custom House
notes.b: The war reached its most violent point in the winter of 1920-21. Then in May 1921 the IRA suffered a heavy loss.
points: On Bloody Sunday, 21 November 1920, the Squad killed 14 men, mostly British officers and intelligence agents, in Dublin.
That afternoon Auxiliaries and RIC opened fire on the crowd at a football match at Croke Park, killing 14 civilians, including a player, Michael Hogan.

At Kilmichael, Co. Cork, on 28 November 1920, Tom Barry's column killed 17 Auxiliaries and lost three men. This was the same week as Croke Park, but it was an IRA ambush of Auxiliaries, not a British killing of civilians.
In May 1921 the IRA burned the Custom House in Dublin but lost five men killed and about 80 captured, a heavy blow to the Dublin Brigade.
About 2,000 people were killed in the war, including soldiers, police, IRA men and civilians, though estimates vary.
notes.tip: Bloody Sunday 1920 means Dublin, the Squad then Croke Park, not Derry in 1972 or the 1913 lockout. Do not confuse Kilmichael (IRA ambush) with Croke Park (British fire on civilians).

notes.b: Britain reinforced the police and the army, but its harsher methods turned opinion against it instead of beating the IRA.
points: The Black and Tans were ex-soldiers recruited as temporary RIC constables. Because of a shortage of police uniforms they wore a mix of khaki and dark green, which gave them their nickname; they began arriving in March 1920 and about 10,000 served.

The Auxiliary Division of the RIC (ADRIC), about 2,000 ex-officers, was formed in July 1920. Unlike the Tans, it operated in companies with considerable independence. This is why they were a separate force from the Tans.

The Restoration of Order in Ireland Act (August 1920) allowed courts-martial (military trials) for civilians, and martial law (rule by the army) was declared in several southern counties from December 1920.

Reprisals (revenge attacks on civilians) included the sacking of Balbriggan in September 1920 and the burning of Cork city centre on the night of 11-12 December 1920, after an IRA ambush at Dillon's Cross. Auxiliaries and Black and Tans were blamed.
The Labour Party, the press and many Church leaders in Britain criticised the reprisals, and the Liberal and Labour leaders called for talks. International opinion also turned against them.
notes.tip: Keep the Black and Tans (ex-soldiers, temporary RIC constables) separate from the Auxiliaries (ADRIC, ex-officers). Do not quote a death toll for either.

notes.b: By mid-1921 politics, not just fighting, was pushing both sides towards talks. The Truce followed within weeks of the first formal invitation.
points: The Government of Ireland Act of 1920 set up a Northern parliament (and a Southern one). The elections of May 1921 confirmed Sinn Féin's hold on the south and unionist control in the north-east.
In June 1921 George V opened the Northern parliament and called for reconciliation, and Lloyd George, the British prime minister, invited de Valera to talks on 24 June.
The Truce (a halt to the fighting) began on 11 July 1921.

Britain went to the negotiating table for several reasons. Reprisals damaged its reputation, the IRA could not be crushed without a much larger force, dominion premiers (leaders of self-governing countries of the Empire) and American opinion urged a settlement, and the cost of the war was rising.
De Valera spent June 1919 to December 1920 in the United States raising money and seeking recognition for the republic.
notes.tip: Strong answers explain why Britain negotiated rather than just narrating the war, and separate the military reasons from the political ones. A short question asks what ended on 11 July 1921.

notes.b: Collins was the organiser of the IRA's intelligence war and of the republican finances. He was a participant in the Rising and the war and then a negotiator of the Treaty.
points: Collins (1890-1922) was born near Clonakilty, Co. Cork. He worked in London in the post office and then in a financial firm from 1906 to 1916, and joined the IRB there.
He fought in the GPO in 1916 as aide to Joseph Plunkett and was interned at Frongoch, where he built a network of future activists.
After his release he rose in the Volunteers, the IRB and Sinn Féin. He organised the National Aid funds (support for the families of those killed or jailed) and spoke at Ashe's funeral.
He was Minister for Finance from April 1919, organised the Dáil Loan, and as Director of Intelligence ran the Squad and the spy network. This is why money, as well as guns, was central to his role.
He escaped capture throughout the war and was the most wanted man in Ireland. This made him a symbol of the IRA's survival.
After the Truce he went on to negotiate the Treaty, so the war years were the first half of his career. Because he was both soldier and negotiator, this made him central to the later split.
Contemporaries: republicans admired him as the man who won the war, while British officials regarded him as a ruthless organiser of killing. Churchill and others came to respect him in London.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan (1990) portrayed a hero of the revolution, while Peter Hart (2005) gave a more critical account of the killings in which he was involved.
notes.tip: For a profile, name his roles with dates: Finance from April 1919 and Director of Intelligence. End with one view, such as Coogan's hero against Hart's more critical account.

notes.b: De Valera held the movement together as the leader of Sinn Féin and the Dáil before the Treaty talks. This part covers only the years 1917-1921.
points: De Valera (1882-1975) was born in New York and raised in Bruree, Co. Limerick. He was a maths teacher who joined the Volunteers in 1913.
He commanded the garrison at Boland's Mill in 1916, and his death sentence was commuted, partly because he was born in America. That is why he survived when most of the other leaders were shot.
He was released in June 1917 under the amnesty, won East Clare in July, and became president of Sinn Féin and of the Volunteers in October 1917.
He was arrested in the German Plot in May 1918, escaped from Lincoln on 3 February 1919, and was elected head of the Dáil as Príomh Aire in April 1919.
He was in America from June 1919 to December 1920, where his disputes with the Irish-American leaders John Devoy and Judge Cohalan limited his success.
After his return he took the lead in the talks with Lloyd George in the summer of 1921.
Contemporaries: supporters saw him as the leader who held the movement together, while critics said he was rigid and out of touch with the IRA's campaign.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan (1993) and Diarmaid Ferriter (Judging Dev, 2007) debate whether he was a pragmatist (willing to compromise) or an ideologue (bound by principle).
notes.tip: For a profile, give his roles with dates: Sinn Féin and Volunteers president (October 1917), Príomh Aire (April 1919), then the talks of 1921. Add one contemporary or historian's view.

notes.b: This part covers Markievicz after her release in 1917, as a Sinn Féin politician and Dáil minister. Prison and hiding shaped much of her career in these years.
points: After her release in June 1917 under the amnesty she joined Sinn Féin and the Volunteers' public campaign, and she was elected to the executive.
She was arrested in the German Plot of May 1918 and held in Holloway, where she was elected in December 1918, so she could not take her seat even if she had wished to. She was released in March 1919.

She was Minister for Labour in the Dáil ministry from April 1919 to January 1922, the only woman in the cabinet and one of the first women in Europe to hold cabinet rank. This was a historic first, so it is a common exam fact.
In September 1920 she was arrested again and sentenced to two years' hard labour; she was released in July 1921, after the Truce.
Her work as minister was limited because she was in jail or on the run for much of the time.
She later opposed the Treaty in the Dáil vote in January 1922.
Contemporaries admired her bravery but some Sinn Féin colleagues distrusted her socialism and her flamboyance.
Historians now emphasise her importance as a pioneer of women's participation in revolutionary politics.
notes.tip: For a profile, name her roles with dates: elected from Holloway in December 1918 and Minister for Labour from April 1919. Add one contemporary or historian's view.

notes.h: Assessment: the Sinn Féin mandate and the War of Independence
notes.b: Judgements depend on whether the 1918 election, the Dáil and the IRA are credited with winning the settlement or blamed for its costs. Examiners reward answers that weigh both sides.
points: Achievement: the 1918 result gave Sinn Féin a democratic mandate, and the counter-state showed that Irish people could run their own affairs.
Achievement: the IRA campaign made Ireland costly and hard to govern and, with Dáil publicity abroad, brought Britain to talks.
Limit: the IRA never controlled much territory, and it was small, short of arms and under strain by mid-1921.

Limit: the election was won on about 47 per cent of the votes, with many seats uncontested. It was a vote for a republic or against the IPP, not an approval of every IRA act, and the war involved violence and the intimidation of informers.
Contemporary view: nationalists saw a legitimate government defending itself, while the British government at first treated the IRA as a criminal conspiracy before changing course.
Later view: historians debate how far the war was supported by the majority and how far it involved intimidation of informers and loyalists, as in Peter Hart's work on Cork.
The dual strategy of Dáil and IRA left the movement with two sources of authority, which left it open to the split over the Treaty in 1922.
notes.tip: Attach each view to a named group or historian: the British government and nationalists as contemporaries, and Coogan, Hart and Ferriter later. Strong essays judge how much was owed to British mistakes and how much to Sinn Féin's own organisation.

keyTerms.definition: A state without a monarch as its head, which Sinn Féin and the Dáil claimed for Ireland from 1917 and 1919.
Supreme authority over a state's own affairs, which the Dáil claimed in its Declaration of Independence in 1919.
The Irish Republican Brotherhood was the secret republican society; the Irish Republican Army was the Volunteers' name from 1919, owing allegiance to the Dáil from August 1920.
The party founded by Griffith in 1905 on abstention and self-reliance, reorganised in 1917 around the demand for a republic.
The policy of refusing to take seats at Westminster, adopted by Sinn Féin MPs after 1918.
The 1918 threat to extend military service to Ireland, which united nationalists in opposition and boosted Sinn Féin.
The British government's claim in May 1918 that Sinn Féin was conspiring with Germany, used to arrest its leaders.
The assembly of Sinn Féin MPs that met on 21 January 1919 and claimed to be the legitimate parliament of Ireland.
The social programme adopted by the First Dáil in 1919, giving priority to the nation's right to its resources over private property.
A small mobile IRA unit that ambushed forces and then dispersed, the main fighting unit of the War of Independence.
Two groups of ex-servicemen added to the RIC in 1920: the Tans as temporary constables and the Auxiliaries as an ex-officers' division.
The ceasefire that began on 11 July 1921 and made negotiations possible.
